results.title: Army Breaks Up Missile Supply Chain to Cut Interceptor Costs Below $1 Million
results.snippet: The Low-Cost Interceptor program, formally launched at an Industry Day on June 23, 2026, in Arlington, Virginia, is the Army's answer to that structural gap. The LCI program's most consequential architectural decision is not about the interceptor itself. It is about who owns the interceptor. Rather than awarding a single prime contractor the right to design, build, and sell a finished weapon — the traditional defense acquisition model that has historically concentrated both cost control and technical decision-making in one vendor — the Army is decomposing the supply chain into separately competed subsegments: solid rocket motors, seekers, fire control and flight guidance systems, and a Weapon System Integrator responsible for designing the open systems architecture that ties them together.

results.title: MDA awards X-Bow to develop low-cost interceptor | DefenseScoop
results.snippet: By comparison, a single Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptor costs roughly $12.7 million, while a Patriot missile has an average price tag of $4 million. During phase 2 of the LCI program, X-Bow will build and flight test a prototype of the weapon. Afterwards, the company is expected to deliver four-to-10 systems that MDA can use for intercept tests, according to the solicitation. X-Bow primarily builds solid rocket motors (SRM) — a critical supply component of munitions.
